Vadim Marmer, UBC

Endogeneity

Endogenous and exogenous regressors

  • Regression, k = k_1 + k_2: Y_i = \underset{1 \times k_1}{X_{i,1}^\top}\ \underset{k_1 \times 1}{\beta_1} + \underset{1 \times k_2}{X_{i,2}^\top}\ \underset{k_2 \times 1}{\beta_2} + U_i

  • X_{i,1} endogenous: \mathrm{E}\left[X_{i,1} U_i\right] \ne 0

  • X_{i,2} exogenous: \mathrm{E}\left[X_{i,2} U_i\right] = 0

Omitted variables

  • Log wage on education: \log \text{Wage}_i = \beta_1\, \text{Education}_i + X_{i,2}^\top \beta_2 + U_i

  • X_{i,2}: exogenous, for example gender.

  • Ability: unobserved, in the error: U_i = \text{ability}_i + \varepsilon_i

  • \varepsilon_i: luck.

  • Education chosen optimally by i given ability: \mathrm{E}\left[\text{Education}_i \times \text{ability}_i\right] \ne 0 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \text{Education}_i \ \text{ endogenous}

Simultaneity: demand and supply

  • Market i, demand and supply: \begin{aligned} \underset{1 \times 1}{Y_i^d} &= \beta_1 P_i + \beta_2 I_i + U_i^d, \qquad \beta_1 < 0 \\ Y_i^s &= \gamma_1 P_i + \gamma_2 G_i + U_i^s, \qquad \gamma_1 > 0 \end{aligned}

  • I_i: observed demand shifter (e.g. income).

  • G_i: observed supply shifter (e.g. input prices, weather).

  • U_i^d, U_i^s: unobserved demand and supply shifters.

  • Y_i^d, Y_i^s: not observed.

  • Observed in equilibrium: Y_i = Y_i^d = Y_i^s, \qquad P_i : \ \text{equilibrium price}

Equilibrium price

  • Supply equals demand; solve for P_i: \begin{aligned} \underbrace{\gamma_1 P_i + \gamma_2 G_i + U_i^s}_{Y_i^s} &= \underbrace{\beta_1 P_i + \beta_2 I_i + U_i^d}_{Y_i^d} \\ (\gamma_1 - \beta_1) P_i &= -\gamma_2 G_i + \beta_2 I_i + U_i^d - U_i^s \\ P_i &= \underbrace{\frac{-\gamma_2}{\gamma_1 - \beta_1}}_{\pi_1} G_i + \underbrace{\frac{\beta_2}{\gamma_1 - \beta_1}}_{\pi_2} I_i + \frac{U_i^d - U_i^s}{\gamma_1 - \beta_1} \end{aligned}

  • Common denominator in P_i: \gamma_1 - \beta_1 > 0

Price and the demand error

  • Demand regression: Y_i = \beta_1 P_i + \beta_2 I_i + U_i^d

  • Assume: U_i^d, U_i^s uncorrelated with G_i, I_i and with each other: \mathrm{E}\left[G_i U_i^d\right] = 0, \qquad \mathrm{E}\left[I_i U_i^d\right] = 0, \qquad \mathrm{E}\left[U_i^s U_i^d\right] = 0

  • Substitute the equilibrium price: \begin{aligned} \mathrm{E}\left[P_i U_i^d\right] &= \mathrm{E}\left[\Big(\pi_1 G_i + \pi_2 I_i + \frac{U_i^d - U_i^s}{\gamma_1 - \beta_1}\Big) U_i^d\right] \\ &= \mathrm{E}\left[\pi_1 G_i U_i^d + \pi_2 I_i U_i^d + \frac{(U_i^d)^2 - U_i^s U_i^d}{\gamma_1 - \beta_1}\right] \\ &= \pi_1 \underbrace{\mathrm{E}\left[G_i U_i^d\right]}_{=\,0} + \pi_2 \underbrace{\mathrm{E}\left[I_i U_i^d\right]}_{=\,0} + \frac{\mathrm{E}\left[(U_i^d)^2\right] - \overbrace{\mathrm{E}\left[U_i^s U_i^d\right]}^{=\,0}}{\gamma_1 - \beta_1} \\ &= \frac{\mathrm{E}\left[(U_i^d)^2\right]}{\gamma_1 - \beta_1} > 0 \end{aligned}

  • P_i: endogenous in the demand equation.

OLS under endogeneity

OLS estimator of \beta_1

  • One endogenous regressor, k_1 = 1: Y_i = \underset{1 \times 1}{\beta_1}\, \underset{1 \times 1}{X_{i,1}} + X_{i,2}^\top \beta_2 + U_i, \qquad \mathrm{E}\left[X_{i,1} U_i\right] \ne 0, \qquad \mathrm{E}\left[X_{i,2} U_i\right] = 0

  • M_2 = I_n - X_2 (X_2^\top X_2)^{-1} X_2^\top.

  • Recall, partitioned regression: \begin{aligned} \hat\beta_1 &= (X_1^\top M_2 \underset{n \times 1}{X_1})^{-1} X_1^\top M_2 Y \\ &= \frac{X_1^\top M_2 Y}{X_1^\top M_2 X_1} \\ &= \beta_1 + \frac{\frac{1}{n} X_1^\top M_2 U}{\frac{1}{n} X_1^\top M_2 X_1} \qquad (M_2 X_2 = 0) \end{aligned}

Denominator of \hat\beta_1 - \beta_1

  • Assume:
    • (Y_i, X_i) iid.
    • \mathrm{E}\left[\|X_i\|^2\right] < \infty.
    • \mathrm{E}\left[U_i^2\right] < \infty.
  • Recall:
    • Weak LLN for sample averages.
    • Slutsky for products and inverses.
  • Expand M_2, take limits: \begin{aligned} \underbrace{\frac{1}{n} X_1^\top M_2 X_1}_{1 \times 1} &= \frac{X_1^\top X_1}{n} - \frac{X_1^\top X_2}{n} \Big(\frac{X_2^\top X_2}{n}\Big)^{-1} \frac{X_2^\top X_1}{n} \\ &\to_p \underbrace{\mathrm{E}\left[X_{i,1}^2\right]}_{Q_{11}} - \underbrace{\mathrm{E}\left[X_{i,1} X_{i,2}^\top\right]}_{Q_{12}}\ \underbrace{\big(\mathrm{E}\left[X_{i,2} X_{i,2}^\top\right]\big)^{-1}}_{Q_{22}^{-1}}\ \underbrace{\mathrm{E}\left[X_{i,2} X_{i,1}\right]}_{Q_{21}} \\ &= Q_{1 \cdot 2} > 0 \qquad (\mathrm{E}\left[X_i X_i^\top\right] \ \text{p.d.}) \end{aligned}

Numerator of \hat\beta_1 - \beta_1

  • Weak LLN; expand M_2, take limits: \begin{aligned} \frac{X_1^\top U}{n} &= \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n X_{i,1} U_i \\ &\to_p \mathrm{E}\left[X_{i,1} U_i\right] \\ \frac{1}{n} X_1^\top M_2 U &= \frac{X_1^\top U}{n} - \frac{X_1^\top X_2}{n} \Big(\frac{X_2^\top X_2}{n}\Big)^{-1} \frac{X_2^\top U}{n} \\ &\to_p \mathrm{E}\left[X_{i,1} U_i\right] - Q_{12}\, Q_{22}^{-1} \underbrace{\mathrm{E}\left[X_{i,2} U_i\right]}_{=\,0} \\ &= \mathrm{E}\left[X_{i,1} U_i\right] \ne 0 \end{aligned}

Asymptotic bias of \hat\beta_1

  • Slutsky: \begin{aligned} \hat\beta_1 &= \beta_1 + \frac{\frac{1}{n} X_1^\top M_2 U}{\frac{1}{n} X_1^\top M_2 X_1} \\ &\to_p \beta_1 + \frac{\overbrace{\mathrm{E}\left[X_{i,1} U_i\right]}^{\ne\, 0}}{Q_{1 \cdot 2}} \ne \beta_1 \end{aligned}

  • Asymptotic bias of OLS: \boxed{\ \mathrm{AsyBias}(\hat\beta_1) = \frac{\mathrm{E}\left[X_{i,1} U_i\right]}{Q_{1 \cdot 2}}\ }

  • Wage example, X_{i,1}: education, U_i: ability: \mathrm{E}\left[X_{i,1} U_i\right] > 0 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \mathrm{AsyBias}(\hat\beta_1) > 0

  • \hat\beta_1 over-estimates \beta_1.

OLS estimator of \beta_2

  • M_1 = I_n - X_1 (X_1^\top X_1)^{-1} X_1^\top.

  • Coefficients on the exogenous regressors: \begin{aligned} \hat\beta_2 &= (X_2^\top M_1 X_2)^{-1} X_2^\top M_1 Y \\ &= \beta_2 + \Big(\frac{X_2^\top M_1 X_2}{n}\Big)^{-1} \frac{X_2^\top M_1 U}{n} \end{aligned}

  • First factor, inside the inverse: \frac{X_2^\top M_1 X_2}{n} \to_p Q_{2 \cdot 1} = Q_{22} - Q_{21}\, Q_{11}^{-1} Q_{12} \qquad \text{p.d.}

  • Second factor: \begin{aligned} \frac{X_2^\top M_1 U}{n} &= \underbrace{\frac{X_2^\top U}{n}}_{\to_p\, \mathrm{E}\left[X_{i,2} U_i\right] \,=\, 0} - \underbrace{\frac{X_2^\top X_1}{n}}_{\to_p\, Q_{21}}\ \underbrace{\Big(\frac{X_1^\top X_1}{n}\Big)^{-1}}_{\to_p\, Q_{11}^{-1}}\ \underbrace{\frac{X_1^\top U}{n}}_{\to_p\, \mathrm{E}\left[X_{i,1} U_i\right] \,\ne\, 0} \\ &\to_p -Q_{21}\, Q_{11}^{-1}\, \mathrm{E}\left[X_{i,1} U_i\right] \end{aligned}

Asymptotic bias of \hat\beta_2

  • Q_{11} = \mathrm{E}\left[X_{i,1}^2\right]: scalar.

  • Slutsky: \begin{aligned} \hat\beta_2 &\to_p \beta_2 - \underbrace{Q_{2 \cdot 1}^{-1}}_{\text{p.d.}} Q_{21}\, Q_{11}^{-1}\, \mathrm{E}\left[X_{i,1} U_i\right] \\ &= \beta_2 - \frac{Q_{2 \cdot 1}^{-1}}{Q_{11}}\, Q_{21}\, \mathrm{E}\left[X_{i,1} U_i\right] \end{aligned}

  • \hat\beta_2: asymptotically biased unless Q_{21} = \mathrm{E}\left[X_{i,2} X_{i,1}\right] = 0

Example: education and gender

  • Wage equation, U_i: ability: \log \text{Wage}_i = \beta_1\, \underbrace{\text{Education}_i}_{X_{i,1}} + \beta_2\, \underbrace{\text{Female}_i}_{X_{i,2},\ \text{dummy}} + U_i

  • Suppose: \mathrm{E}\left[X_{i,1} U_i\right] > 0, \qquad Q_{21} = \mathrm{E}\left[\text{Female}_i\, \text{Education}_i\right] > 0

  • Asymptotic bias of \hat\beta_1: \hat\beta_1 - \beta_1 \to_p \underbrace{Q_{1 \cdot 2}^{-1}}_{+}\ \underbrace{\mathrm{E}\left[X_{i,1} U_i\right]}_{+} > 0

  • Asymptotic bias of \hat\beta_2: \hat\beta_2 - \beta_2 \to_p -\underbrace{Q_{2 \cdot 1}^{-1}}_{+}\ \underbrace{Q_{21}}_{+}\ \underbrace{Q_{11}^{-1}}_{+}\ \underbrace{\mathrm{E}\left[X_{i,1} U_i\right]}_{+} < 0

Identification and instruments

Identification without endogeneity

  • No endogeneity: Y_i = X_i^\top \beta + U_i, \qquad \beta \in \mathbb{R}^k, \qquad \mathrm{E}\left[X_i U_i\right] = 0

  • Moment condition: k equations in k unknowns.

  • Assume \mathrm{E}\left[X_i X_i^\top\right] invertible: \begin{aligned} & \mathrm{E}\left[X_i \overbrace{(Y_i - X_i^\top \beta)}^{U_i}\right] = 0 \\ \Longleftrightarrow\quad & \underbrace{\mathrm{E}\left[X_i Y_i\right]}_{k \times 1} = \underbrace{\mathrm{E}\left[X_i X_i^\top\right]}_{k \times k}\ \underset{k \times 1}{\beta} \\ \Longrightarrow\quad & \beta = \big(\mathrm{E}\left[X_i X_i^\top\right]\big)^{-1} \mathrm{E}\left[X_i Y_i\right] \qquad \text{(identification)} \end{aligned}

  • Both moments estimated by sample averages: \begin{aligned} \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n X_i X_i^\top &\to_p \mathrm{E}\left[X_i X_i^\top\right] \\ \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n X_i Y_i &\to_p \mathrm{E}\left[X_i Y_i\right] \end{aligned}

  • Slutsky: \begin{aligned} \hat\beta &= \Big(\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n X_i X_i^\top\Big)^{-1} \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n X_i Y_i \\ &\to_p \big(\mathrm{E}\left[X_i X_i^\top\right]\big)^{-1} \mathrm{E}\left[X_i Y_i\right] = \beta \qquad \text{(consistency)} \end{aligned}

Identification with endogeneity

  • X_{i,1} endogenous: k_1 equations lost: \mathrm{E}\left[X_{i,1} U_i\right] \ne 0, \qquad \mathrm{E}\left[X_{i,2} U_i\right] = 0

  • Remaining moment condition: \mathrm{E}\left[\underset{k_2 \times 1}{X_{i,2}} \big(Y_i - X_{i,1}^\top \underset{k_1 \times 1}{\beta_1} - X_{i,2}^\top \underset{k_2 \times 1}{\beta_2}\big)\right] = 0

  • k_2 equations, k_1 + k_2 unknowns \Longrightarrow no unique solution for \beta_1, \beta_2: not identified.

Instrumental variables (IVs)

  • Suppose we also observe Z_{i,1}, an \ell_1 \times 1 vector of variables such that: \mathrm{E}\left[Z_{i,1} U_i\right] = 0 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \ell_1 \ \text{ additional equations}

  • Two sets of moment conditions: \begin{aligned} \mathrm{E}\left[X_{i,2} (Y_i - X_{i,1}^\top \beta_1 - X_{i,2}^\top \beta_2)\right] &= 0 \qquad (k_2 \ \text{equations}) \\ \mathrm{E}\left[Z_{i,1} (Y_i - X_{i,1}^\top \beta_1 - X_{i,2}^\top \beta_2)\right] &= 0 \qquad (\ell_1 \ \text{equations}) \end{aligned}

Stacked moment condition

  • Regressors X_i and exogenous variables (IVs) Z_i: \begin{aligned} X_i &= \begin{pmatrix} X_{i,1} \\ X_{i,2} \end{pmatrix} : \ \underbrace{(k_1 + k_2)}_{=\,k} \times 1 \\ Z_i &= \begin{pmatrix} Z_{i,1} \\ X_{i,2} \end{pmatrix} : \ \underbrace{(\ell_1 + k_2)}_{=\,\ell} \times 1 \\ \beta &= \begin{pmatrix} \beta_1 \\ \beta_2 \end{pmatrix} \end{aligned}

  • Two sets of moment conditions: \begin{aligned} \mathrm{E}\left[X_{i,2} (Y_i - X_{i,1}^\top \beta_1 - X_{i,2}^\top \beta_2)\right] &= 0 \qquad (k_2 \ \text{equations}) \\ \mathrm{E}\left[Z_{i,1} (Y_i - X_{i,1}^\top \beta_1 - X_{i,2}^\top \beta_2)\right] &= 0 \qquad (\ell_1 \ \text{equations}) \end{aligned}

  • Moment condition: \begin{aligned} & \mathrm{E}\left[Z_i (Y_i - X_i^\top \beta)\right] = 0 \\ \Longleftrightarrow\quad & \underbrace{\mathrm{E}\left[Z_i X_i^\top\right]}_{\ell \times k}\ \underset{k \times 1}{\beta} = \underbrace{\mathrm{E}\left[Z_i Y_i\right]}_{\ell \times 1} \end{aligned}

  • \ell = \ell_1 + k_2 equations, k = k_1 + k_2 unknowns.

One regressor, one instrument

  • Simplified version, Y_i, X_i, U_i, Z_i all 1 \times 1: Y_i = \beta X_i + U_i

  • Covariance with the instrument: \begin{aligned} \mathrm{Cov}\left(Z_i, Y_i\right) &= \beta\, \mathrm{Cov}\left(Z_i, X_i\right) + \overbrace{\mathrm{Cov}\left(Z_i, U_i\right)}^{=\,0} \\ \Longrightarrow\quad \beta &= \frac{\mathrm{Cov}\left(Z_i, Y_i\right)}{\mathrm{Cov}\left(Z_i, X_i\right)} \qquad \text{if } \ \mathrm{Cov}\left(Z_i, X_i\right) \ne 0 \end{aligned}

Exactly identified case: IV estimator

  • \ell = k (\ell_1 = k_1): k equations in k unknowns.

  • Assume \mathrm{E}\left[Z_i X_i^\top\right] has rank k: \begin{aligned} \underbrace{\mathrm{E}\left[Z_i X_i^\top\right]}_{k \times k}\ \underset{k \times 1}{\beta} &= \underbrace{\mathrm{E}\left[Z_i Y_i\right]}_{k \times 1} \\ \Longrightarrow\quad \beta &=\boxed{\ \big(\mathrm{E}\left[Z_i X_i^\top\right]\big)^{-1} \mathrm{E}\left[Z_i Y_i\right]\ } \end{aligned}

  • Sample averages in place of expectations: \begin{aligned} \hat\beta^{IV} &= \Big(\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n Z_i X_i^\top\Big)^{-1} \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n Z_i Y_i \\ &= \Big(\sum_{i=1}^n Z_i X_i^\top\Big)^{-1} \sum_{i=1}^n Z_i Y_i \\ &= (Z^\top X)^{-1} Z^\top Y \end{aligned}

  • Z: n \times \ell, with rows Z_i^\top, as X with rows X_i^\top: \begin{aligned} Z &= \begin{pmatrix} Z_1^\top \\ \vdots \\ Z_n^\top \end{pmatrix} \\ \sum_{i=1}^n Z_i X_i^\top &= Z^\top X \\ \sum_{i=1}^n Z_i Y_i &= Z^\top Y \end{aligned}

Over-identified case

  • \ell > k (\ell_1 > k_1): more equations than unknowns.

  • Premultiply by \mathrm{E}\left[X_i Z_i^\top\right], which is k \times \ell: \begin{aligned} & \underbrace{\mathrm{E}\left[Z_i X_i^\top\right]}_{\ell \times k}\ \underset{k \times 1}{\beta} = \underbrace{\mathrm{E}\left[Z_i Y_i\right]}_{\ell \times 1} \\ \Longrightarrow\quad & \underbrace{\big(\mathrm{E}\left[X_i Z_i^\top\right]\big) \big(\mathrm{E}\left[Z_i X_i^\top\right]\big)}_{k \times k}\ \underset{k \times 1}{\beta} = \underbrace{\big(\mathrm{E}\left[X_i Z_i^\top\right]\big) \mathrm{E}\left[Z_i Y_i\right]}_{k \times 1} \\ \Longrightarrow\quad & \beta = \Big[\big(\mathrm{E}\left[X_i Z_i^\top\right]\big) \big(\mathrm{E}\left[Z_i X_i^\top\right]\big)\Big]^{-1} \big(\mathrm{E}\left[X_i Z_i^\top\right]\big) \mathrm{E}\left[Z_i Y_i\right] \end{aligned}

  • Condition for identification: k \times k inverse exists.

Rank condition

  • The \ell \times k matrix Q: Q = \mathrm{E}\left[Z_i X_i^\top\right], \qquad Q^\top = \mathrm{E}\left[X_i Z_i^\top\right]

  • Rank condition. \operatorname{rank}\left(Q\right) = \operatorname{rank}\left(\mathrm{E}\left[Z_i X_i^\top\right]\right) = k

  • \operatorname{rank}\left(Q\right) = k \Longrightarrow Q^\top Q p.d.

  • For c \in \mathbb{R}^k and v = Qc: \begin{aligned} c^\top Q^\top Q c &= v^\top v \\ &= \|v\|^2 \\ &> 0 \quad \text{unless } c = 0 \qquad (v = Qc \ne 0 \ \text{ unless } c = 0) \end{aligned}

  • Rank condition: necessary and sufficient for identification of \beta.

Order condition

  • Definition of Q: \underset{\ell \times k}{Q} = \mathrm{E}\left[\underset{\ell \times 1}{Z_i}\ \underset{1 \times k}{X_i^\top}\right]

  • Necessary for the rank condition: \begin{aligned} \operatorname{rank}\left(\underset{\ell \times k}{Q}\right) = k \quad &\Longrightarrow \quad \ell \ge k \\ &\Longleftrightarrow \quad \ell_1 + k_2 \ge k_1 + k_2 \\ &\Longleftrightarrow \quad \underbrace{\ell_1}_{\text{number of IVs}} \ge \underbrace{k_1}_{\text{number of endogenous regressors}} \end{aligned}

  • Three cases: \begin{aligned} \operatorname{rank}\left(Q\right) = k, \ \ell = k &: \ \text{exactly identified} \\ \operatorname{rank}\left(Q\right) = k, \ \ell > k &: \ \text{over-identified} \\ \operatorname{rank}\left(Q\right) < k &: \ \text{under-identified} \quad (\ell < k, \ \text{or linear dependence}) \end{aligned}

Exclusion restriction

  • Two scalar regressors: Y_i = \beta_1 X_{i,1} + \beta_2 X_{i,2} + U_i, \qquad \mathrm{E}\left[X_{i,2} U_i\right] = 0

  • Try Z_{i,1} = X_{i,2}: \begin{aligned} \underset{2 \times 2}{\mathrm{E}\left[Z_i X_i^\top\right]} &= \mathrm{E}\left[\begin{pmatrix} Z_{i,1} \\ X_{i,2} \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} X_{i,1} & X_{i,2} \end{pmatrix}\right] \\ &= \begin{pmatrix} \mathrm{E}\left[Z_{i,1} X_{i,1}\right] & \mathrm{E}\left[Z_{i,1} X_{i,2}\right] \\ \mathrm{E}\left[X_{i,2} X_{i,1}\right] & \mathrm{E}\left[X_{i,2} X_{i,2}\right] \end{pmatrix} \\ &= \begin{pmatrix} \mathrm{E}\left[X_{i,2} X_{i,1}\right] & \mathrm{E}\left[X_{i,2} X_{i,2}\right] \\ \mathrm{E}\left[X_{i,2} X_{i,1}\right] & \mathrm{E}\left[X_{i,2} X_{i,2}\right] \end{pmatrix} \qquad (Z_{i,1} = X_{i,2}) \end{aligned}

  • Two equal rows \Longrightarrow rank 1 < k = 2.

  • Exclusion restriction: Z_{i,1} excluded from the equation for Y_i.

  • No direct effect of Z_{i,1} on Y_i.

Relevance restriction

  • Suppose Z_{i,1} is “noise”, with \mathrm{E}\left[Z_{i,1} U_i\right] = 0: \mathrm{E}\left[Z_i X_i^\top\right] = \begin{pmatrix} \overbrace{\mathrm{E}\left[Z_{i,1} X_{i,1}\right]}^{=\,0} & \overbrace{\mathrm{E}\left[Z_{i,1} X_{i,2}\right]}^{=\,0} \\ \mathrm{E}\left[X_{i,2} X_{i,1}\right] & \mathrm{E}\left[X_{i,2} X_{i,2}\right] \end{pmatrix}

  • Row of zeros \Longrightarrow rank 1 < k = 2.

First stage and the rank condition

First stage

  • First stage, for the endogenous regressors: \underset{k_1 \times 1}{X_{i,1}} = \underset{k_1 \times \ell_1}{{\color{red} \Pi_1^\top}}\ \underset{\ell_1 \times 1}{Z_{i,1}} + \underset{k_1 \times k_2}{\Pi_2^\top}\ \underset{k_2 \times 1}{X_{i,2}} + \underset{k_1 \times 1}{V_i}

  • V_i uncorrelated with Z_{i,1} and X_{i,2}: \mathrm{E}\left[Z_{i,1} V_i^\top\right] = 0, \qquad \mathrm{E}\left[X_{i,2} V_i^\top\right] = 0

  • V_i correlated with U_i \Longrightarrow X_{i,1} endogenous.

  • First stage in terms of Z_i, with \Pi: \ell \times k_1: X_{i,1} = \Pi^\top Z_i + V_i, \qquad \Pi = \begin{pmatrix} {\color{red} \Pi_1} \\ \Pi_2 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \mathrm{E}\left[Z_i V_i^\top\right] = 0

  • Claim. With \mathrm{E}\left[Z_i Z_i^\top\right] p.d.: \operatorname{rank}\left(\mathrm{E}\left[Z_i X_i^\top\right]\right) = k \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \operatorname{rank}\left({\color{red} \Pi_1}\right) = k_1

  • Interpretation of the rank condition: excluded variables Z_{i,1} informative about the endogenous regressors.

Proof, step 1: \mathrm{E}\left[Z_i X_i^\top\right] in blocks

  • We will use the transposed first stage: X_{i,1}^\top = Z_{i,1}^\top \Pi_1 + X_{i,2}^\top \Pi_2 + V_i^\top

  • \mathrm{E}\left[Z_{i,1} V_i^\top\right] = 0, \mathrm{E}\left[X_{i,2} V_i^\top\right] = 0.

  • Write in blocks; substitute the first stage: \begin{aligned} \mathrm{E}\left[Z_i X_i^\top\right] &= \mathrm{E}\left[\begin{pmatrix} Z_{i,1} \\ X_{i,2} \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} X_{i,1}^\top & X_{i,2}^\top \end{pmatrix}\right] \\ &= \begin{pmatrix} \mathrm{E}\left[Z_{i,1} X_{i,1}^\top\right] & \mathrm{E}\left[Z_{i,1} X_{i,2}^\top\right] \\ \mathrm{E}\left[X_{i,2} X_{i,1}^\top\right] & \mathrm{E}\left[X_{i,2} X_{i,2}^\top\right] \end{pmatrix} \\ &= \begin{pmatrix} \mathrm{E}\left[Z_{i,1} Z_{i,1}^\top\right] \Pi_1 + \mathrm{E}\left[Z_{i,1} X_{i,2}^\top\right] \Pi_2 & \mathrm{E}\left[Z_{i,1} X_{i,2}^\top\right] \\ \mathrm{E}\left[X_{i,2} Z_{i,1}^\top\right] \Pi_1 + \mathrm{E}\left[X_{i,2} X_{i,2}^\top\right] \Pi_2 & \mathrm{E}\left[X_{i,2} X_{i,2}^\top\right] \end{pmatrix} \end{aligned}

Proof, step 2: \mathrm{E}\left[Z_i X_i^\top\right] \theta

  • Multiply by \theta = \begin{pmatrix} \theta_1 \\ \theta_2 \end{pmatrix}, with \theta_1: k_1 \times 1 and \theta_2: k_2 \times 1: \begin{aligned} \mathrm{E}\left[Z_i X_i^\top\right] \theta &= \begin{pmatrix} \big(\mathrm{E}\left[Z_{i,1} Z_{i,1}^\top\right] \Pi_1 + \mathrm{E}\left[Z_{i,1} X_{i,2}^\top\right] \Pi_2\big) \theta_1 + \mathrm{E}\left[Z_{i,1} X_{i,2}^\top\right] \theta_2 \\ \big(\mathrm{E}\left[X_{i,2} Z_{i,1}^\top\right] \Pi_1 + \mathrm{E}\left[X_{i,2} X_{i,2}^\top\right] \Pi_2\big) \theta_1 + \mathrm{E}\left[X_{i,2} X_{i,2}^\top\right] \theta_2 \end{pmatrix} \\ &= \begin{pmatrix} \mathrm{E}\left[Z_{i,1} Z_{i,1}^\top\right] \Pi_1 \theta_1 + \mathrm{E}\left[Z_{i,1} X_{i,2}^\top\right] (\Pi_2 \theta_1 + \theta_2) \\ \mathrm{E}\left[X_{i,2} Z_{i,1}^\top\right] \Pi_1 \theta_1 + \mathrm{E}\left[X_{i,2} X_{i,2}^\top\right] (\Pi_2 \theta_1 + \theta_2) \end{pmatrix} \\ &= \underbrace{\begin{pmatrix} \mathrm{E}\left[Z_{i,1} Z_{i,1}^\top\right] & \mathrm{E}\left[Z_{i,1} X_{i,2}^\top\right] \\ \mathrm{E}\left[X_{i,2} Z_{i,1}^\top\right] & \mathrm{E}\left[X_{i,2} X_{i,2}^\top\right] \end{pmatrix}}_{=\, \mathrm{E}\left[Z_i Z_i^\top\right], \ \ell \times \ell, \ \text{p.d.}} \begin{pmatrix} \Pi_1 \theta_1 \\ \Pi_2 \theta_1 + \theta_2 \end{pmatrix} \end{aligned}

Proof, step 3: sufficiency of \operatorname{rank}\left(\Pi_1\right) = k_1

  • \mathrm{E}\left[Z_i Z_i^\top\right] p.d.

  • Suppose \operatorname{rank}\left(\Pi_1\right) = k_1: \begin{aligned} \mathrm{E}\left[Z_i X_i^\top\right] \theta = 0 \quad &\Longleftrightarrow \quad \Pi_1 \theta_1 = 0 \ \text{ and } \ \Pi_2 \theta_1 + \theta_2 = 0 \\ &\Longleftrightarrow \quad \theta_1 = 0 \ \text{ and } \ \Pi_2 \theta_1 + \theta_2 = 0 \qquad (\operatorname{rank}\left(\Pi_1\right) = k_1) \\ &\Longleftrightarrow \quad \theta_1 = 0 \ \text{ and } \ \theta_2 = 0 \\ &\Longleftrightarrow \quad \theta = 0 \end{aligned}

  • k columns of \mathrm{E}\left[Z_i X_i^\top\right] linearly independent: \operatorname{rank}\left(\Pi_1\right) = k_1 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \operatorname{rank}\left(\mathrm{E}\left[Z_i X_i^\top\right]\right) = k

Proof, step 4: necessity of \operatorname{rank}\left(\Pi_1\right) = k_1

  • Suppose \operatorname{rank}\left(\Pi_1\right) < k_1: \begin{aligned} & \text{there is } \ \theta_1 \ne 0 \ \text{ such that } \ \Pi_1 \theta_1 = 0 \\ & \text{define } \ \theta_2 = -\Pi_2 \theta_1 \\ \Longrightarrow\quad & \Pi_2 \theta_1 + \theta_2 = 0 \\ \Longrightarrow\quad & \mathrm{E}\left[Z_i Z_i^\top\right] \begin{pmatrix} \Pi_1 \theta_1 \\ \Pi_2 \theta_1 + \theta_2 \end{pmatrix} = 0 \\ \Longrightarrow\quad & \mathrm{E}\left[Z_i X_i^\top\right] \theta = 0 \quad \text{with } \ \theta \ne 0 \\ \Longrightarrow\quad & \operatorname{rank}\left(\mathrm{E}\left[Z_i X_i^\top\right]\right) < k \end{aligned}

  • Hence: \operatorname{rank}\left(\mathrm{E}\left[Z_i X_i^\top\right]\right) = k \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \operatorname{rank}\left(\Pi_1\right) = k_1

Requirements for instruments

  • We need Z_{i,1}: \ell_1 \times 1, with \ell_1 \ge k_1, such that:

    1. Z_{i,1} excluded from the equation for Y_i.
    2. Z_{i,1} exogenous: \mathrm{E}\left[Z_{i,1} U_i\right] = 0.
    3. Z_{i,1} informative about X_{i,1}: \operatorname{rank}\left(\Pi_1\right) = k_1 in the first stage.

  • Wage example, U_i: ability.

  • IV must be:

    1. Independent of ability.
    2. Not affecting the wage directly.
    3. Shifting education.

One endogenous regressor

  • Suppose k_1 = 1.

  • For example, Y_i = \log \text{Wage}_i and X_{i,1} = \text{Education}_i: \underset{1 \times 1}{\text{Education}_i} = \underset{1 \times \ell_1}{\Pi_1^\top}\ \underset{\ell_1 \times 1}{Z_{i,1}} + \Pi_2^\top X_{i,2} + V_i, \qquad \Pi_1 = \begin{pmatrix} \Pi_{1,1} \\ \vdots \\ \Pi_{1,\ell_1} \end{pmatrix}

  • First stage written instrument by instrument: X_{i,1} = \sum_{j=1}^{\ell_1} Z_{i,1,j}\, \Pi_{1,j} + \Pi_2^\top X_{i,2} + V_i

  • Rank condition: \begin{aligned} \operatorname{rank}\left(\Pi_1\right) = 1 \quad &\Longleftrightarrow \quad \Pi_1 \ne 0 \\ &\Longleftrightarrow \quad \Pi_{1,j} \ne 0 \ \text{ for at least one } j = 1, \ldots, \ell_1 \end{aligned}

Example: Angrist and Krueger (1991)

  • Angrist, J. D. and A. B. Krueger (1991). “Does Compulsory School Attendance Affect Schooling and Earnings?” Quarterly Journal of Economics 106(4), 979–1014.

  • Wage equation: \log \text{Wage}_i = \beta_1\, \text{Education}_i + X_{i,2}^\top \beta_2 + U_i

  • X_{i,2}: year-of-birth and region dummies, race, marital status, urban residence, age, age^2.

  • IVs: quarter-of-birth dummies, Z_{i,1}.

  • First stage: \text{Education}_i = Z_{i,1}^\top \Pi_1 + X_{i,2}^\top \Pi_2 + V_i

  • Born early in the year \Longrightarrow older at school start \Longrightarrow less schooling at the compulsory leaving age.

  • Hence \Pi_1 \ne 0.

Demand and supply: instruments

  • Demand and supply: \begin{aligned} Y_i^d &= \beta_1 P_i + \beta_2 I_i + U_i^d, \qquad \beta_1 < 0 \\ Y_i^s &= \gamma_1 P_i + \gamma_2 G_i + U_i^s, \qquad \gamma_1 > 0 \end{aligned}

  • G_i excluded from demand, but G_i affects the price: P_i = \underbrace{\frac{-\gamma_2}{\gamma_1 - \beta_1}}_{\pi_1 \,\ne\, 0 \ \text{if} \ \gamma_2 \,\ne\, 0} G_i + \frac{\beta_2}{\gamma_1 - \beta_1} I_i + \frac{U_i^d - U_i^s}{\gamma_1 - \beta_1}

  • Exogenous: \mathrm{E}\left[G_i U_i^d\right] = 0.

  • Hence G_i: IV for P_i in the demand equation.

  • Changing G_i shifts the supply curve:

  • Equilibria lie on one demand curve \Longrightarrow demand curve identified.

Example: Angrist and Evans (1998)

  • Angrist, J. D. and W. N. Evans (1998). “Children and Their Parents’ Labor Supply: Evidence from Exogenous Variation in Family Size.” American Economic Review 88(3), 450–477.

  • Married women with at least 2 children: \begin{aligned} \text{Hours worked}_i &= \beta_1\, \text{Number of children}_i + X_{i,2}^\top \beta_2 + U_i \\ \text{Number of children}_i &= \gamma_1\, \text{Hours worked}_i + \gamma_2\, \text{Same sex}_i + X_{i,2}^\top \gamma_3 + U_i^c \end{aligned}

  • X_{i,2}: mother’s age, age at first birth, race, sex of first and second child.

  • \text{Same sex}_i = 1 if the first two children are both boys or both girls.

  • IV for \text{Number of children}_i: \text{Same sex}_i.

  • First stage: \text{Number of children}_i = \Pi_1\, \text{Same sex}_i + X_{i,2}^\top \Pi_2 + V_i

  • First two children of the same sex \Longrightarrow third child more likely.

  • Hence \Pi_1 > 0.

Generalized method of moments (GMM)

Weight matrix W

  • Definition. Weight matrix W: \ell \times \ell, symmetric, p.d.

  • Premultiply by Q^\top W: \begin{aligned} Q\, \beta &= \mathrm{E}\left[Z_i Y_i\right] \\ \Longrightarrow\quad \underbrace{\underset{k \times \ell}{Q^\top}\ \underset{\ell \times \ell}{W}\ \underset{\ell \times k}{Q}}_{k \times k}\ \beta &= Q^\top W\, \mathrm{E}\left[Z_i Y_i\right] \\ \Longrightarrow\quad \beta &= (Q^\top W Q)^{-1} Q^\top W\, \mathrm{E}\left[Z_i Y_i\right] \end{aligned}

  • W = I_\ell \Longrightarrow \beta = (Q^\top Q)^{-1} Q^\top \mathrm{E}\left[Z_i Y_i\right].

Exactly identified case: W cancels

  • \ell = k.

  • Q, W: k \times k, invertible: \begin{aligned} \beta &= (\underset{k \times k}{Q^\top}\ \underset{k \times k}{W}\ \underset{k \times k}{Q})^{-1}\, \underset{k \times k}{Q^\top}\ \underset{k \times k}{W}\, \mathrm{E}\left[Z_i Y_i\right] \\ &= Q^{-1}\, {\color{red} W^{-1} (Q^\top)^{-1} Q^\top W}\, \mathrm{E}\left[Z_i Y_i\right] \\ &= Q^{-1}\, \mathrm{E}\left[Z_i Y_i\right] \end{aligned}

  • Sample averages in place of expectations: \begin{aligned} (X^\top Z\, W\, Z^\top X)^{-1} X^\top Z\, W\, Z^\top Y &= (Z^\top X)^{-1} Z^\top Y \\ &= \hat\beta^{IV} \end{aligned}

GMM estimator \hat\beta(W_n)

  • Definition. GMM estimator with weight matrix W_n: \hat\beta(W_n) = (X^\top Z\, W_n\, Z^\top X)^{-1} X^\top Z\, W_n\, Z^\top Y

  • Assumption I.

    • \{(Y_i, X_i, Z_i) : i = 1, \ldots, n\} iid.
    • Y_i = X_i^\top \beta + U_i, \beta \in \mathbb{R}^k.

  • Assumption II. \mathrm{E}\left[Z_i U_i\right] = 0.

  • Assumption III. \operatorname{rank}\left(Q\right) = k, Q = \mathrm{E}\left[Z_i X_i^\top\right].

  • Assumption IV.

    • W_n \to_p W.
    • W: \ell \times \ell, symmetric, p.d.

Consistency of \hat\beta(W_n)

  • Weak LLN, Assumptions I and II: \begin{aligned} \frac{Z^\top X}{n} &= \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n Z_i X_i^\top \to_p \mathrm{E}\left[Z_i X_i^\top\right] = Q \\ \frac{Z^\top U}{n} &= \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n Z_i U_i \to_p \mathrm{E}\left[Z_i U_i\right] = 0 \end{aligned}

  • Slutsky, Assumptions III and IV: \Big(\frac{X^\top Z}{n}\, W_n\, \frac{Z^\top X}{n}\Big)^{-1} \to_p (Q^\top W Q)^{-1}

  • Theorem. Under Assumptions I to IV: \begin{aligned} \hat\beta(W_n) &= \beta + (X^\top Z\, W_n\, Z^\top X)^{-1} X^\top Z\, W_n\, Z^\top U \qquad (Y = X\beta + U) \\ &= \beta + \underbrace{\Big(\frac{X^\top Z}{n}\, W_n\, \frac{Z^\top X}{n}\Big)^{-1}}_{\to_p\, (Q^\top W Q)^{-1}}\ \underbrace{\frac{X^\top Z}{n}\, W_n}_{\to_p\, Q^\top W}\ \underbrace{\frac{Z^\top U}{n}}_{\to_p\, 0} \\ &\to_p \beta \end{aligned}

CLT for Z^\top U / \sqrt{n}

  • Assumption V. \Omega = \mathrm{E}\left[U_i^2 Z_i Z_i^\top\right] finite and p.d.

  • Variance of Z_i U_i, with \mathrm{E}\left[Z_i U_i\right] = 0: \begin{aligned} \Omega &= \mathrm{Var}\left(Z_i U_i\right) \\ &= \mathrm{E}\left[Z_i U_i (Z_i U_i)^\top\right] \\ &= \mathrm{E}\left[U_i^2 Z_i Z_i^\top\right] \end{aligned}

  • Z_1 U_1, \ldots, Z_n U_n: iid.

  • Multivariate CLT: \frac{Z^\top U}{\sqrt{n}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \sum_{i=1}^n Z_i U_i \to_d N(0, \Omega)

Asymptotic variance of \hat\beta(W_n)

  • Recall, Cramér convergence theorem: A_n \to_p A, A non-random, B_n \to_d B \Longrightarrow A_n B_n \to_d A B.

  • Multiply the representation of \hat\beta(W_n) - \beta by \sqrt{n}: \begin{aligned} \sqrt{n}\big(\hat\beta(W_n) - \beta\big) &= \underbrace{\Big(\frac{X^\top Z}{n}\, W_n\, \frac{Z^\top X}{n}\Big)^{-1}}_{\to_p\, (Q^\top W Q)^{-1}}\ \underbrace{\frac{X^\top Z}{n}\, W_n}_{\to_p\, Q^\top W}\ \underbrace{\frac{Z^\top U}{\sqrt{n}}}_{\to_d\, N(0, \Omega)} \\ &\to_d (Q^\top W Q)^{-1} Q^\top W\, N(0, \Omega) \\ &\overset{d}{=} N\big(0,\ \underbrace{(Q^\top W Q)^{-1} Q^\top W \Omega W Q (Q^\top W Q)^{-1}}_{V(W)}\big) \qquad (W,\ Q^\top W Q \ \text{symmetric}) \end{aligned}

  • Theorem. Under Assumptions I to V: \sqrt{n}\big(\hat\beta(W_n) - \beta\big) \to_d N\big(0, V(W)\big), \qquad V(W) = \mathrm{AsyVar}\big(\hat\beta(W_n)\big)

Efficient weight matrix W^* = \Omega^{-1}

  • Definition. Efficient weight matrix W^*: minimizes V(W) in the p.s.d. sense: V(W) - V(W^*) \ge 0 \quad \text{(p.s.d.) for every } W

  • Claim. W^* = \Omega^{-1}.

  • V(W) at W = \Omega^{-1}: \begin{aligned} V(\Omega^{-1}) &= (Q^\top \Omega^{-1} Q)^{-1}\ \underbrace{Q^\top \Omega^{-1} \Omega\, \Omega^{-1} Q}_{=\, Q^\top \Omega^{-1} Q}\ (Q^\top \Omega^{-1} Q)^{-1} \\ &= (Q^\top \Omega^{-1} Q)^{-1} \end{aligned}

  • W^* = \Omega^{-1} matters only if \ell > k.

  • \ell = k \Longrightarrow W cancels.

Comparing asymptotic variances

  • Scalars, a, b > 0: a - b \ge 0 \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \frac{1}{b} - \frac{1}{a} \ge 0

  • Matrices, p.s.d. differences: \begin{aligned} & V(W) - V(\Omega^{-1}) \ge 0 \\ \Longleftrightarrow\quad & \big(V(\Omega^{-1})\big)^{-1} - \big(V(W)\big)^{-1} \ge 0 \end{aligned}

Proof that W^* = \Omega^{-1} is efficient

  • \Omega p.d. \Longrightarrow \Omega^{1/2}: symmetric, \Omega^{1/2}\, \Omega^{1/2} = \Omega.

  • \Omega^{-1/2} = (\Omega^{1/2})^{-1}.

  • Recall: M_H = I - H (H^\top H)^{-1} H^\top: symmetric, idempotent, p.s.d.

  • Difference of the inverses: \begin{aligned} \big(V(\Omega^{-1})\big)^{-1} - \big(V(W)\big)^{-1} &= Q^\top \Omega^{-1} Q - (Q^\top W Q)(Q^\top W \Omega W Q)^{-1}(Q^\top W Q) \\ &= Q^\top \Omega^{-1/2} \Big(I - \underbrace{\Omega^{1/2} W Q}_{H}\, \big(\underbrace{Q^\top W \Omega W Q}_{H^\top H}\big)^{-1} \underbrace{Q^\top W \Omega^{1/2}}_{H^\top}\Big) \Omega^{-1/2} Q \\ &= Q^\top \Omega^{-1/2}\, \underbrace{M_H}_{\text{p.s.d.}}\, \Omega^{-1/2} Q \\ &\ge 0 \end{aligned}

Two-step efficient GMM

  • Efficient weight matrix, unknown: W^* = \Omega^{-1} = \big(\mathrm{E}\left[U_i^2 Z_i Z_i^\top\right]\big)^{-1}

  • Step 1: W_n = I_\ell.

  • \hat\beta(I_\ell) consistent.

  • Estimator of \Omega from the residuals of \hat\beta(I_\ell): \hat\Omega_n = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \big(Y_i - X_i^\top \hat\beta(I_\ell)\big)^2 Z_i Z_i^\top

  • Step 2: W_n = \hat\Omega_n^{-1}, efficient GMM: \hat\beta(\hat\Omega_n^{-1}) = (X^\top Z\, \hat\Omega_n^{-1} Z^\top X)^{-1} X^\top Z\, \hat\Omega_n^{-1} Z^\top Y

  • One can show: \hat\Omega_n \to_p \Omega.

Asymptotic variance of \hat\beta^{IV}

  • \ell = k.

  • Q: k \times k, invertible.

  • IV estimator: \begin{aligned} \hat\beta^{IV} &= (\underbrace{Z^\top X}_{k \times k})^{-1} Z^\top Y \\ &= \beta + (Z^\top X)^{-1} Z^\top U \qquad (Y = X\beta + U) \end{aligned}

  • Cramér convergence theorem: \begin{aligned} \sqrt{n}\big(\hat\beta^{IV} - \beta\big) &= \underbrace{\Big(\frac{Z^\top X}{n}\Big)^{-1}}_{\to_p\, Q^{-1}}\ \underbrace{\frac{Z^\top U}{\sqrt{n}}}_{\to_d\, N(0, \Omega)} \\ &\to_d Q^{-1}\, N(0, \Omega) \end{aligned}

  • We will use: (Q^{-1})^\top = (Q^\top)^{-1}.

  • Variance of Q^{-1} N(0, \Omega): \begin{aligned} \mathrm{AsyVar}\big(\hat\beta^{IV}\big) &= Q^{-1}\, \Omega\, (Q^{-1})^\top \\ &= \boxed{\ \big(\mathrm{E}\left[Z_i X_i^\top\right]\big)^{-1}\, \mathrm{E}\left[U_i^2 Z_i Z_i^\top\right]\, \big(\mathrm{E}\left[X_i Z_i^\top\right]\big)^{-1}\ } \end{aligned}

Two-stage least squares (2SLS)

Homoskedasticity: efficient GMM is 2SLS

  • Suppose: \mathrm{E}\left[U_i^2 \mid Z_i\right] = \sigma^2 \quad \text{(homoskedasticity)}

  • Law of iterated expectations (LIE): \begin{aligned} \Omega &= \mathrm{E}\left[U_i^2 Z_i Z_i^\top\right] \\ &\overset{\text{LIE}}{=} \sigma^2\, \mathrm{E}\left[Z_i Z_i^\top\right] \end{aligned}

  • Estimator of \Omega: \hat\Omega_n = \hat\sigma_n^2\, \frac{Z^\top Z}{n}

  • Efficient GMM: \begin{aligned} \hat\beta(\hat\Omega_n^{-1}) &= \Big(X^\top Z \Big(\hat\sigma_n^2\, \frac{Z^\top Z}{n}\Big)^{-1} Z^\top X\Big)^{-1} X^\top Z \Big(\hat\sigma_n^2\, \frac{Z^\top Z}{n}\Big)^{-1} Z^\top Y \\ &= \big(X^\top \underbrace{Z (Z^\top Z)^{-1} Z^\top}_{P_Z} X\big)^{-1} X^\top \underbrace{Z (Z^\top Z)^{-1} Z^\top}_{P_Z} Y \\ &= \boxed{\ (X^\top P_Z X)^{-1} X^\top P_Z Y \equiv \hat\beta^{2SLS}\ } \end{aligned}

  • The scalar n / \hat\sigma_n^2 cancels.

2SLS: first and second stage

  • First stage, OLS of X_{i,1} on Z_i: \begin{aligned} \hat\Pi &= (Z^\top Z)^{-1} Z^\top X_1 \\ \hat X_{i,1} &= \hat\Pi^\top Z_i \\ &= \hat\Pi_1^\top Z_{i,1} + \hat\Pi_2^\top X_{i,2} \end{aligned}

  • X_2: columns of Z \Longrightarrow P_Z X_2 = X_2.

  • Fitted values: \begin{aligned} \hat X &= P_Z X \\ \hat X_i &= \begin{pmatrix} \hat X_{i,1} \\ X_{i,2} \end{pmatrix} \end{aligned}

  • We will use: P_Z = P_Z^\top P_Z.

  • Second stage, OLS of Y on \hat X: \begin{aligned} \hat\beta^{2SLS} &= (X^\top P_Z X)^{-1} X^\top P_Z Y \\ &= (\hat X^\top \hat X)^{-1} \hat X^\top Y \end{aligned}

Control function and the Hausman test

Every regressor endogenous

  • k_2 = 0: X_i = X_{i,1}, Z_i = Z_{i,1}.

  • Model and first stage, \Pi: \ell \times k: \begin{aligned} Y_i &= X_i^\top \beta + U_i \\ \underset{k \times 1}{X_i} &= \underset{k \times \ell}{\Pi^\top}\, \underset{\ell \times 1}{Z_i} + \underset{k \times 1}{V_i} \end{aligned}

  • Exogenous instruments: \mathrm{E}\left[Z_i U_i\right] = 0

  • \Pi defined so that Z_i, V_i uncorrelated: \mathrm{E}\left[Z_i V_i^\top\right] = 0

  • V_i: the source of endogeneity: \mathrm{E}\left[X_i U_i\right] \ne 0, \quad \mathrm{E}\left[Z_i U_i\right] = 0 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \mathrm{E}\left[V_i U_i\right] \ne 0

Decomposition of U_i

  • Define: \begin{aligned} \lambda &= \big(\mathrm{E}\left[V_i V_i^\top\right]\big)^{-1} \mathrm{E}\left[V_i U_i\right] \\ \varepsilon_i &= U_i - V_i^\top \lambda \\ \Longrightarrow\quad U_i &= V_i^\top \lambda + \varepsilon_i \end{aligned}

  • V_i and \varepsilon_i uncorrelated: \begin{aligned} \mathrm{E}\left[V_i \varepsilon_i\right] &= \mathrm{E}\left[V_i U_i\right] - \mathrm{E}\left[V_i V_i^\top\right] \lambda \\ &= \mathrm{E}\left[V_i U_i\right] - {\color{red} \mathrm{E}\left[V_i V_i^\top\right] \big(\mathrm{E}\left[V_i V_i^\top\right]\big)^{-1}} \mathrm{E}\left[V_i U_i\right] \\ &= 0 \end{aligned}

Augmented regression and control function

  • Z_i and \varepsilon_i uncorrelated: \begin{aligned} \mathrm{E}\left[Z_i \varepsilon_i\right] &= \mathrm{E}\left[Z_i (U_i - V_i^\top \lambda)\right] \\ &= \underbrace{\mathrm{E}\left[Z_i U_i\right]}_{=\,0} - \underbrace{\mathrm{E}\left[Z_i V_i^\top\right]}_{=\,0} \lambda \\ &= 0 \end{aligned}

  • X_i and \varepsilon_i uncorrelated: \begin{aligned} \mathrm{E}\left[X_i \varepsilon_i\right] &= \mathrm{E}\left[(\Pi^\top Z_i + V_i)\, \varepsilon_i\right] \\ &= \Pi^\top \underbrace{\mathrm{E}\left[Z_i \varepsilon_i\right]}_{=\,0} + \underbrace{\mathrm{E}\left[V_i \varepsilon_i\right]}_{=\,0} \\ &= 0 \end{aligned}

  • Substitute U_i = V_i^\top \lambda + \varepsilon_i: \begin{aligned} Y_i &= X_i^\top \beta + V_i^\top \lambda + \varepsilon_i \\ \mathrm{E}\left[X_i \varepsilon_i\right] &= 0 \\ \mathrm{E}\left[V_i \varepsilon_i\right] &= 0 \end{aligned}

  • No endogeneity.

  • V_i: control function.

Control function (CF) estimator

  • First-stage residuals: \hat V_i = X_i - \hat\Pi^\top Z_i, \qquad \hat\Pi = (Z^\top Z)^{-1} Z^\top X

  • CF estimator, OLS of Y_i on X_i and \hat V_i: Y_i = X_i^\top \hat\beta^{CF} + \hat V_i^\top \hat\lambda + \hat\varepsilon_i

  • Claim. \hat\beta^{CF} = \hat\beta^{2SLS}.

Proof that \hat\beta^{CF} = \hat\beta^{2SLS}

  • We will use: Z \hat\Pi = P_Z X.

  • Matrix form: \underset{n \times 1}{Y} = \underset{n \times k}{X} \hat\beta^{CF} + \hat V \hat\lambda + \hat\varepsilon, \qquad \hat V = X - Z \hat\Pi = M_Z X

  • M_{\hat V} = I_n - \hat V (\hat V^\top \hat V)^{-1} \hat V^\top.

  • Recall, partitioned regression: \hat\beta^{CF} = (X^\top M_{\hat V} X)^{-1} X^\top M_{\hat V} Y

  • M_Z symmetric, idempotent \Longrightarrow \hat V^\top \hat V = X^\top M_Z X: \begin{aligned} X^\top M_{\hat V} X &= X^\top X - X^\top \hat V (\hat V^\top \hat V)^{-1} \hat V^\top X \\ &= X^\top X - X^\top M_Z X\, {\color{red} (X^\top M_Z X)^{-1} X^\top M_Z X} \\ &= X^\top (I_n - M_Z) X \\ &= X^\top P_Z X \end{aligned}

  • Same steps, with Y in place of the last X: X^\top M_{\hat V} Y = X^\top P_Z Y

  • Hence: \boxed{\ \hat\beta^{CF} = (X^\top P_Z X)^{-1} X^\top P_Z Y = \hat\beta^{2SLS}\ }

Hausman test of exogeneity

  • \hat\lambda: estimator of \lambda = \big(\mathrm{E}\left[V_i V_i^\top\right]\big)^{-1} \mathrm{E}\left[V_i U_i\right].

  • Exogeneity of the regressors in terms of \lambda: \begin{aligned} \lambda = 0 \quad &\Longleftrightarrow \quad \mathrm{E}\left[V_i U_i\right] = 0 \\ &\Longleftrightarrow \quad \mathrm{E}\left[X_i U_i\right] = 0 \qquad (\mathrm{E}\left[X_i U_i\right] = \Pi^\top \mathrm{E}\left[Z_i U_i\right] + \mathrm{E}\left[V_i U_i\right]) \end{aligned}

  • Hypotheses: H_0: \lambda = 0 \ \ (X_i \ \text{exogenous}) \qquad \text{vs} \qquad H_1: \lambda \ne 0 \ \ (X_i \ \text{endogenous})

  • Under H_0, one can show: H_n = n\, \hat\lambda^\top \big[\widehat{\mathrm{AsyVar}}(\hat\lambda)\big]^{-1} \hat\lambda \to_d \chi^2_{k_1}, \qquad k_1: \ \text{number of endogenous regressors}

  • Reject H_0: H_n > \chi^2_{k_1,\, 1-\alpha}.

Over-identifying restrictions test

Exactly identified case: Z^\top \hat U = 0

  • Linear IV model, \beta \in \mathbb{R}^k, Z_i \in \mathbb{R}^\ell: Y_i = X_i^\top \beta + U_i, \qquad \mathrm{E}\left[Z_i U_i\right] = 0, \qquad \operatorname{rank}\left(\mathrm{E}\left[Z_i X_i^\top\right]\right) = k

  • \ell = k.

  • \hat U = Y - X \hat\beta^{IV}: \begin{aligned} Z^\top \hat U &= Z^\top Y - Z^\top X \hat\beta^{IV} \\ &= Z^\top Y - {\color{red} Z^\top X (Z^\top X)^{-1}} Z^\top Y \\ &= 0 \end{aligned}

Hypotheses and efficient GMM

  • \ell > k: \begin{aligned} H_0 &: \ \mathrm{E}\left[Z_i (Y_i - X_i^\top \beta)\right] = 0 \quad \text{for some } \beta \in \mathbb{R}^k \\ H_1 &: \ \mathrm{E}\left[Z_i (Y_i - X_i^\top b)\right] \ne 0 \quad \text{for all } b \in \mathbb{R}^k \end{aligned}

  • \hat\beta = \hat\beta(\hat\Omega_n^{-1}): efficient GMM.

  • \hat\Omega_n \to_p \Omega: \Omega = \mathrm{E}\left[U_i^2 Z_i Z_i^\top\right] = \mathrm{E}\left[(Y_i - X_i^\top \beta)^2 Z_i Z_i^\top\right]

Statistic J

  • \hat U_i = Y_i - X_i^\top \hat\beta.

  • \hat\Omega_n^{-1}-weighted distance of \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n Z_i \hat U_i from zero: \begin{aligned} J &= \frac{1}{n} (Y - X\hat\beta)^\top Z\ \hat\Omega_n^{-1}\ \frac{1}{n} Z^\top (Y - X\hat\beta) \\ &= \Big(\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n Z_i \hat U_i\Big)^\top \hat\Omega_n^{-1} \Big(\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n Z_i \hat U_i\Big) \end{aligned}

  • \ell = k: \hat\beta = \hat\beta^{IV}, Z^\top \hat U = 0 \Longrightarrow J = 0, whether H_0 is true or false.

  • \ell > k, H_0 true: \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n Z_i \hat U_i \to_p 0 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad J > 0, \ \text{but} \ J \to_p 0

Quadratic form at the true \beta

  • Under H_0, CLT: \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} Z^\top (Y - X\beta) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \sum_{i=1}^n Z_i U_i \to_d N(0, \Omega)

  • We will use, for x \in \mathbb{R}^\ell: \begin{aligned} x^\top \Omega^{-1} x &= x^\top \Omega^{-1/2}\, \Omega^{-1/2} x \\ &= (\Omega^{-1/2} x)^\top\, \Omega^{-1/2} x \\ &= \|\Omega^{-1/2} x\|^2 \end{aligned}

  • \mathcal{Z} = \Omega^{-1/2} N(0, \Omega) \sim N(0, I_\ell): \begin{aligned} \|\mathcal{Z}\|^2 &= \mathcal{Z}^\top \mathcal{Z} \\ &= \sum_{j=1}^\ell \mathcal{Z}_j^2 \sim \chi^2_\ell \end{aligned}

  • \hat\Omega_n^{-1} = \Omega^{-1} + o_p(1): \begin{aligned} \frac{(Y - X\beta)^\top Z}{\sqrt{n}}\, \hat\Omega_n^{-1}\, \frac{Z^\top (Y - X\beta)}{\sqrt{n}} &= \frac{U^\top Z}{\sqrt{n}}\, \Omega^{-1}\, \underbrace{\frac{Z^\top U}{\sqrt{n}}}_{\to_d\, N(0, \Omega)} + o_p(1) \\ &= \Big\|\underbrace{\Omega^{-1/2}\, \frac{Z^\top U}{\sqrt{n}}}_{\to_d\, \mathcal{Z}}\Big\|^2 + o_p(1) \\ &\to_d \|\mathcal{Z}\|^2 \sim \chi^2_\ell \end{aligned}

J test and Sargan’s test

  • Under H_0, one can show, with \hat\beta efficient GMM: nJ = \frac{(Y - X\hat\beta)^\top Z}{\sqrt{n}}\, \hat\Omega_n^{-1}\, \frac{Z^\top (Y - X\hat\beta)}{\sqrt{n}} \to_d \chi^2_{\ell - k}

  • k IVs used to estimate \beta, \ell - k IVs used to test.

  • Test: reject H_0 when nJ > \chi^2_{\ell - k,\, 1-\alpha}.

  • \mathrm{E}\left[U_i^2 \mid Z_i\right] = \sigma^2 \Longrightarrow \hat\Omega_n = \hat\sigma_n^2\, \frac{Z^\top Z}{n}, \hat\beta = \hat\beta^{2SLS}.

  • Then J test: Sargan’s test.

Constructing more instruments

Functions of exogenous variables as instruments

  • Suppose: \mathrm{E}\left[U_i \mid X_{i,2}, Z_{i,1}\right] = 0

  • Law of iterated expectations, any function h: \begin{aligned} \mathrm{E}\left[h(X_{i,2}, Z_{i,1})\, U_i\right] &= \mathrm{E}\left[\mathrm{E}\left[h(X_{i,2}, Z_{i,1})\, U_i \mid X_{i,2}, Z_{i,1}\right]\right] \\ &= \mathrm{E}\left[h(X_{i,2}, Z_{i,1})\, \underbrace{\mathrm{E}\left[U_i \mid X_{i,2}, Z_{i,1}\right]}_{=\,0}\right] \\ &= 0 \end{aligned}

  • Z_{i,1}: IVs \Longrightarrow products of entries of Z_{i,1} and X_{i,2}: IVs too.

Angrist and Krueger instruments

  • X_{i,2}: gender, race, year-of-birth and geographic dummies.

  • Quarter-of-birth dummies: Z_{i,1} = \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{1}(\text{quarter of birth}_i = 1) \\ \mathbf{1}(\text{quarter of birth}_i = 2) \\ \mathbf{1}(\text{quarter of birth}_i = 3) \end{pmatrix}

  • More IVs: each quarter-of-birth dummy times each year-of-birth dummy.

Summary

Endogeneity and identification

  • \mathrm{E}\left[X_{i,1} U_i\right] \ne 0 \Longrightarrow OLS inconsistent.

  • k_1 = 1: \mathrm{AsyBias}(\hat\beta_1) = \mathrm{E}\left[X_{i,1} U_i\right] / Q_{1 \cdot 2}.

  • k_1 = 1: \hat\beta_2 also asymptotically biased unless \mathrm{E}\left[X_{i,2} X_{i,1}\right] = 0.

  • Z_i = (Z_{i,1}^\top, X_{i,2}^\top)^\top.

  • \mathrm{E}\left[Z_i (Y_i - X_i^\top \beta)\right] = 0: \ell equations, k unknowns.

  • Rank condition \operatorname{rank}\left(\mathrm{E}\left[Z_i X_i^\top\right]\right) = k \Longleftrightarrow \operatorname{rank}\left(\Pi_1\right) = k_1.

  • Order condition \ell_1 \ge k_1.

  • Z_{i,1}: excluded, exogenous, informative.

  • \ell = k: \hat\beta^{IV} = (Z^\top X)^{-1} Z^\top Y.

GMM and 2SLS

  • \hat\beta(W_n) = (X^\top Z W_n Z^\top X)^{-1} X^\top Z W_n Z^\top Y.

  • Assumptions I to IV \Longrightarrow \hat\beta(W_n) \to_p \beta.

  • Assumptions I to V \Longrightarrow \sqrt{n}(\hat\beta(W_n) - \beta) \to_d N(0, V(W)).

  • V(W) = (Q^\top W Q)^{-1} Q^\top W \Omega W Q (Q^\top W Q)^{-1}.

  • Efficient weight matrix: W^* = \Omega^{-1}, V(\Omega^{-1}) = (Q^\top \Omega^{-1} Q)^{-1}.

  • Two-step efficient GMM: \hat\Omega_n from \hat\beta(I_\ell).

  • \ell = k \Longrightarrow \hat\beta(W_n) = \hat\beta^{IV}.

  • \mathrm{AsyVar}(\hat\beta^{IV}) = Q^{-1} \Omega (Q^{-1})^\top.

  • \mathrm{E}\left[U_i^2 \mid Z_i\right] = \sigma^2 \Longrightarrow efficient GMM = \hat\beta^{2SLS} = (X^\top P_Z X)^{-1} X^\top P_Z Y = (\hat X^\top \hat X)^{-1} \hat X^\top Y.

  • \hat X = P_Z X.

Control function and specification tests

  • U_i = V_i^\top \lambda + \varepsilon_i: Y_i = X_i^\top \beta + V_i^\top \lambda + \varepsilon_i.

  • \mathrm{E}\left[X_i \varepsilon_i\right] = 0, \mathrm{E}\left[V_i \varepsilon_i\right] = 0.

  • \hat\beta^{CF} = \hat\beta^{2SLS}.

  • Hausman:

    • H_0: \lambda = 0.
    • H_n \to_d \chi^2_{k_1} under H_0.
    • Reject when H_n > \chi^2_{k_1,\, 1-\alpha}.

  • Over-identifying restrictions, \ell > k:

    • nJ \to_d \chi^2_{\ell - k} under H_0.
    • Reject when nJ > \chi^2_{\ell - k,\, 1-\alpha}.
    • Homoskedasticity \Longrightarrow Sargan’s test.

  • \mathrm{E}\left[U_i \mid X_{i,2}, Z_{i,1}\right] = 0 \Longrightarrow \mathrm{E}\left[h(X_{i,2}, Z_{i,1})\, U_i\right] = 0: functions of X_{i,2}, Z_{i,1} as IVs.
